source.title: Automated Interpretability and Feature Discovery in Language Models with Agents

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether explanations predict neuron activations on generated test prompts, using test accuracy rather than the original pole-level audit.
record.gate_note: The MLP-neuron validation in Appendix A.9 directly bears on predictive explanation accuracy. The paper's SAE-feature refinement results and its safety-refusal intervention do not measure the claim versions' neuron-job shares or explanation accuracy for raw neurons, so they are not rows. Prior findings attributed to Gao et al. are cited rather than results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on an interpretability agent. Its neuron result (Appendix A.9) reports how well its own FeatureExplainer loop explains neurons that were pre-selected as the top statistical marker per category. The model is a weight-sparse transformer trained to be interpretable, and scoring is binary accuracy on LLM-generated positive and negative prompts. That gives no share of neurons with good explanations in a representative sample (V7) and no test of whether activating-example explanations fail to predict firing (V6). The SAE-feature results concern SAE latents, not neurons. None of the results bear on V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase covers only the appendix. The authors' main conclusion is that agentic hypothesis refinement beats one-shot autointerp on Gemma-2 SAE features, and that FeatureFinder discovers language- and safety-relevant features. They add that the pipeline transfers to raw MLP neurons in a weight-sparse transformer, rediscovering 2 of 4 neurons from Gao et al. and reaching 75% mean validation accuracy (main text says 'over 75%'). They attribute this accuracy to cleaner activation boundaries in weight-sparse models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an iterative hypothesis-test-refine procedure with LLM-generated test prompts and real MLP activations, rather than a pole-level audit of one-shot explanations. It tests selected neurons in a weight-sparse GPT-2-style transformer.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy varied by category: the authors say unambiguous syntactic markers did best, while context-dependent categories were harder.

fits_no_version.finding: On Gemma-2 SAE features, a refined hypothesis outranks the one-shot top-activating-example autointerp label on 64% (GPT-4o mini), 79% (Gemini 2.5 Pro) and 83% (Claude 4 Sonnet) of features. Case Study 1 shows a baseline label that missed a French-language constraint.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One-shot explanations from top-activating examples of SAE latents often miss constraints that determine activation; iterative hypothesis testing improves them.

fits_no_version.finding: In a weight-sparse transformer, the top marker neurons of 14 Python-syntax categories reach mean accuracy 0.750 (mean AUROC 0.893) on generated test prompts. Context-dependent categories were harder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Selected marker neurons in weight-sparse transformers admit explanations that predict activation on generated prompts with moderate-to-high accuracy.

record.problems: The raw-neuron validation covers selected top neurons from 14 categories in one weight-sparse model; the paper does not state a good-score threshold or uncertainty estimates for the accuracy results.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or job shares.
No neuron job shares in any other dense or MoE model.
No vision neurons and no test of InceptionV1 or recursive generalization versus superposition.
No measurement of the interpretable-neuron share across architectures or tools. The weight-sparse model's cleanliness is asserted, not compared.
No attribution graphs and no neuron-level circuits explaining behaviour.
No test of whether explanations fitted to a neuron's activating examples fail to predict where it fires. The one-shot versus refined comparison is on SAE features only.
No simulation scoring on new text and no share of neurons with good scores in a representative sample. Neurons were selected as top markers.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V6/V7 limits_scope labels are dropped. The rows are the study's own method's performance on neurons pre-selected as top markers, in a model trained to be monosemantic. Neither selected-neuron accuracy nor SAE-latent results can speak to neuron-share or activating-example claims. The reader's per-row states (e.g., 'absent' for accuracy 1.000) had no coherent baseline.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate the shares with one, two, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Does not estimate shares of neuron poles with one or multiple jobs across models or scale.
Does not test the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or recursive generalization versus superposition.
Does not test how architecture, regularization, or tools change the share of interpretable neurons in vision models.
Does not test whether attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons explain behavior without replacement models.

Tests generated explanations on generated positive and negative prompts in one weight-sparse transformer; it does not test the stated activating-example inspection procedure across models or settings.
Reports generated-prompt test accuracy for selected neurons, but does not define a threshold for a 'good' score or estimate the share of neurons meeting such a threshold in a representative sample.

rows.locator: Appendix A.9, Validation with hypothesis testing; Table A10
rows.note: Aggregate over 14 validated neurons. The text also reports that 12 of 14 (86%) exceeded chance level. The paper does not state a threshold for a good score.
rows.check: Mean accuracy 0.750 over the top marker neuron of 14 categories is the study's own method's validation on selected neurons. It is not a representative neuron share, so it cannot show V7's 'minority of neurons'. The hypotheses come from the refine loop, not inspection of activating examples, so it does not test V6. Table A10 also gives mean AUROC 0.893, and 12/14 neurons are above 50%.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Selected MLP neurons in the weight-sparse transformer
reader_labels.reason: Generated explanations had mean test accuracy 75%, with some category results below perfect accuracy (R1, R3–R7); the Try/except result was perfect (R2). This shows varying predictive accuracy rather than a uniform failure.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Top neurons from 14 categories in one weight-sparse transformer
reader_labels.reason: The aggregate mean was 75%, and 12 of 14 neurons exceeded chance, which qualifies a claim of broadly poor test accuracy; the study does not define what counts as a good score, so it cannot determine the share with good scores (R1–R7).
